text: formate to ethylene glycol conversion (Task 11) Our ethylene glycol (EG) production pathway consists of three modules: C1 activation, condensation to glycolyl-CoA (C2), and product synthesis. The C1 utilization module involves the conversion of various carbon sources into formaldehyde and formyl-CoA. The condensation module, catalyzed by Chloroflexi bacterium HGW-Chloroflexi-9 (CfhHACS), facilitates the reaction between formaldehyde and formyl-CoA to produce glycolyl-CoA. In the termination pathway, glycolyl-CoA is converted to glycolaldehyde by aldehyde dehydrogenase, and subsequently, glycolaldehyde is reduced to our target product, ethylene glycol, by glycolaldehyde reductase (Figure 32). Figure 32. Design of the C1 compound utilization pathway for ethylene glycol production. This figure includes three modules: utilization, condensation, and termination. The utilization module includes three different C1 utilization pathways: 1. Formaldehyde as the sole carbon source (highlighted in green), where formaldehyde is converted to formyl-CoA in the presence of ACR. 2. The same as formaldehyde as the sole carbon source, but with formate added 46 as an extra energy source (highlighted in blue); formate is converted to CO2 by formate dehydrogenase (FDH), generating NADH. 3. Methanol as the sole carbon source (highlighted in yellow), where methanol is converted to formaldehyde by methanol dehydrogenase (MDH), and then formaldehyde is converted to formyl-CoA by ACR. The condensation module involves the condensation of formaldehyde and formyl-CoA to produce glycolyl-CoA. The termination module involves the conversion of glycolyl-CoA to glycolaldehyde by Acyl-CoA reductase, and then glycolaldehyde is converted to ethylene glycol by aldehyde dehydrogenase. Crossed lines represent various gene knockouts: Formaldehyde Oxidation (ΔfrmA) Formate Oxidation (ΔfdhF, ΔfdnG, ΔfdoG), Glycolate Dehydrogenase (ΔglcD), Aldehyde Dehydrogenase (ΔaldA, ΔaldB, ΔpUUC, ΔpatD). Thioesterase (ΔyciA, ΔtesA, ΔtesB, ΔybgC, ΔydiI, ΔfadM), Acetate Kinase & Phosphate Acetyltransferase (ΔackA-pta). Other abbreviations: ACR: acyl-CoA reductase, HACS: 2-hydroxyacyl-CoA synthase, MDH: methanol dehydrogenase, FDH: formate dehydrogenase. When formaldehyde serves as the sole carbon source (highlighted in green), producing 1 mol of ethylene glycol requires 2 mol of formaldehyde. One mole of formaldehyde is catalyzed by formyl-CoA reductase (ACR) to form 1 mol of formyl-CoA, which then condenses with another mole of formaldehyde in the termination pathway. However, to achieve 1 mol of ethylene glycol, 2 mol of NADH is required, yet only 1 mol of NADH is generated during the formaldehyde-to-formyl-CoA conversion. Therefore, an additional mole of formaldehyde is necessary to generate sufficient NADH, resulting in a theoretical yield (mol/mol) of 33.3%, equivalent to a 0.69 theoretical yield (g/g). Alternatively, utilizing formate dehydrogenase to convert formate to NADH and CO 2 provides additional NADH supply (highlighted in blue), where formaldehyde serves as the carbon source and formate as the energy source. In this scenario, producing 1 mol of ethylene glycol requires 2 mol of formaldehyde, yielding a theoretical yield (mol/mol) of 50% or 1.03 theoretical yield (g/g). When methanol acts as the sole carbon source, producing 1 mol of ethylene glycol requires 2 mol of methanol. The conversion from glycolyl-CoA to glycolaldehyde requires 1 mol of NADH, while an additional 1 mol of NADH is necessary for the glycolaldehyde to ethylene glycol conversion.
